title: Butyrate-Producing Bacteria and Insulin Homeostasis: The Microbiome and Insulin Longitudinal Evaluation Study (MILES)
claim: Higher Flavonifractor abundance was associated with lower insulin sensitivity and greater prevalence of dysglycemia.
population: African American and non-Hispanic White adults in MILES
limitation: Associations were adjusted for age, sex, BMI and race, but not multiple testing. This does not establish causation or individual clinical risk.

title: Taxonomic and Functional Fecal Microbiota Signatures Associated With Insulin Resistance in Non-Diabetic Subjects With Overweight/Obesity Within the Frame of the PREDIMED-Plus Study
claim: Odoribacter abundance was negatively associated with HOMA-IR, a marker of insulin resistance, in this baseline analysis.
population: Non-diabetic adults aged 55–75 with overweight or obesity and metabolic syndrome in PREDIMED-Plus
limitation: An association in this selected population does not establish that increasing Odoribacter improves insulin sensitivity or that it applies to all populations.

title: Gut microbiome and metabolome profiling in Framingham heart study reveals cholesterol-metabolizing bacteria
claim: Oscillibacter species were associated with lower stool and plasma cholesterol, and cultured human gut isolates metabolized cholesterol in laboratory experiments.
scope: Multiple Oscillibacter species; lipid metabolism rather than direct insulin-resistance evidence
studyType: Human observational multi-omics study plus in vitro isolate experiments
population: Framingham Heart Study participants and cultured human gut isolates
limitation: Cholesterol metabolism does not establish an effect on insulin resistance. Human associations and laboratory activity do not demonstrate treatment benefit.

title: Butyrate-Producing Bacteria and Insulin Homeostasis: The Microbiome and Insulin Longitudinal Evaluation Study (MILES)
claim: Pseudoflavonifractor was not significantly associated with insulin sensitivity or dysglycemia in the reported genus-level analyses.
population: African American and non-Hispanic White adults in MILES
limitation: A null result does not prove no biological effect. It provides useful context if this dataset shows an association; neither finding alone establishes causation.
